clinicalPearls: The eyelid margin turns inward so that lashes rub against the cornea and conjunctiva, causing irritation, foreign body sensation, tearing, and redness
The involutional (age-related) type is the commonest and usually affects the lower lid, driven by tissue laxity
Cicatricial entropion follows conjunctival scarring from conditions such as trachoma, chemical burns, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and ocular cicatricial pemphigoid
Chronic lash-cornea contact risks epithelial breakdown, secondary microbial keratitis, and corneal scarring
Temporary measures include lubrication, taping the lid outward, and botulinum toxin, while lid-everting sutures give short-term relief
Definitive management is surgical correction tailored to the underlying mechanism
Distinguish from trichiasis, where lashes are misdirected but the lid margin itself is correctly positioned
reference.pathophysiology: Entropion is inward rotation of the eyelid margin. Involutional entropion arises from age-related horizontal lid laxity, attenuation or disinsertion of the lower lid retractors, and overriding of the preseptal orbicularis, which together destabilise the lid and allow it to rotate inward. Cicatricial entropion results from contracture of scarred tarsoconjunctiva pulling the margin toward the globe. Spastic entropion is triggered by orbicularis spasm from ocular irritation, and congenital entropion reflects a structural lid defect. In all forms the inturned lashes abrade the ocular surface, causing chronic irritation and potential corneal damage.
additionalDifferentials: Trichiasis (misdirected lashes with normal lid position)
Epiblepharon (extra lower lid skin fold, often in children)
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination to assess lash-cornea contact and corneal integrity
Fluorescein staining to detect epithelial damage
Assessment of horizontal lid laxity (snap-back and distraction tests)
Evaluation of the conjunctival fornices for scarring in suspected cicatricial disease
redFlags: Corneal epithelial defect or infiltrate indicating secondary keratitis and threatened vision
Progressive conjunctival scarring suggesting cicatrising disease such as pemphigoid requiring systemic workup
Persistent lash-cornea contact despite temporising measures
reference.prognosis: Surgical correction is generally effective with good long-term results, though cicatricial cases may recur and require repeated intervention; untreated chronic disease can cause corneal scarring and visual loss.
pitfalls: Treating symptoms with lubricants alone while ongoing lash contact damages the cornea
Failing to identify a cicatricial cause requiring different surgical planning and systemic evaluation
Confusing entropion with trichiasis and choosing the wrong intervention
Overlooking recurrence after involutional repair due to unaddressed lid laxity
management: Definitive surgical correction tailored to the mechanism, with horizontal lid tightening and retractor reattachment for involutional entropion and tarsal or mucous-membrane grafting for cicatricial disease
Ocular surface lubrication with artificial tears and ointment to protect the cornea while awaiting surgery
Temporising measures including taping the lid outward, everting sutures, or botulinum toxin for spastic entropion
Treat the underlying cause of cicatricial disease, such as trachoma or ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, to limit recurrence
Slit-lamp surveillance with fluorescein staining for corneal abrasion and prompt topical antibiotics for secondary microbial keratitis
Ophthalmology referral, anticipating recurrence and the need for repeat surgery in cicatricial cases
